title: Muslim belonging is a dual condition of support, discrimination and representational harm
source_unit: Pew Research Center, Muslims have felt both discrimination and support from other Americans, September 3, 2026
geography: United States; U.S. Muslims, with 2026 measures compared on the chart with selected earlier Pew and Project MAPS measures

observations.period: 2026; current perceptions and experiences among U.S. Muslims

denominator.unit: U.S. Muslim respondents in Pew's American Trends Panel and related historical survey series; chart does not state the 2026 n on the public page

religion_based_support.unit: percent saying someone expressed support in the past year because they are Muslim

perceived_discrimination.unit: percent saying there is a lot of discrimination against Muslims

unfair_tv_movie_portrayal.unit: percent saying Muslims receive unfair portrayal in TV and movies

mechanism.value: Belonging and exclusion can be experienced simultaneously: interpersonal support does not cancel group-level discrimination or representational harm

observations.method: Pew Research Center chart based on the 2026 American Trends Panel and historical Pew telephone surveys; the public chart reports percentages and question wording but not the 2026 sample size on the page.
observations.uncertainty: The measures capture perceptions and reported experiences, not independently verified incidents, causal effects, population prevalence outside the survey frame or changes in institutional treatment.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Muslims with potentially different experiences by age, race, gender, immigration history, geography, religiosity, visibility and media use; those subgroup estimates are not supplied in the public chart.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support and discrimination responses may refer to different settings and social actors; their coexistence does not imply that respondents experience every institution or community as uniformly hostile or supportive.

observations.period: 2001–2026; historical comparison shown by Pew with changing question wording

denominator.unit: historical Pew and Project MAPS survey measures displayed on the chart

series_scope.value: The chart displays selected measures from 2001, 2007, 2011, 2017 and 2026, but the labels and wording are not identical across years

longitudinal_caution.value: The historical display supports a question about persistence and change in perceived discrimination and portrayal, but does not by itself establish a single comparable time series

meaning.value: Representation and everyday treatment remain linked components of group belonging, even when the available indicators change across survey waves

observations.method: Pew chart reproducing current and historical survey measures from the American Trends Panel, Pew telephone surveys and Project MAPS; historical question wording and response frames are displayed in the chart notes.
observations.uncertainty: Different wording, modes, samples and reference periods limit direct trend comparisons; the chart is not a harmonized repeated-measures dataset.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Muslim respondents across survey years, with historical comparability constrained by the available survey instruments.
observations.counterinterpretation: A change in a displayed percentage may reflect wording, mode, sampling or context as well as a change in underlying social conditions.

observations.period: 2026; cultural representation, media trust and public legitimacy

representation_authority.value: When unfair portrayal is reported alongside discrimination, media representation becomes part of how institutional respect and public membership are judged

consumer_cultural_effect.value: Perceived misrepresentation can affect media choice, brand and platform trust, willingness to be publicly visible, and demand for culturally competent services

political_effect.value: The gap between interpersonal support and group-level protection can create pressure for voice, accountability and institutional recognition without implying a single partisan response

observations.method: Interpretive extension of the Pew measures, explicitly separated from the survey's reported percentages.
observations.uncertainty: The chart does not measure media consumption, purchasing, platform behavior, political participation, service use or causal effects of representation.
observations.subgroup: Muslim audiences, media institutions, platforms, brands, schools, employers, public agencies and civic organizations that mediate recognition and everyday belonging.
observations.counterinterpretation: Representation concerns may motivate cultural production and civic participation rather than withdrawal; support networks may buffer harm, and the source does not measure either pathway.

related_sources.claim: Official Pew chart with 2026 percentages, historical comparison display, question notes and source survey description.

boundary: This record identifies a cultural belonging, discrimination, representation and institutional-voice subtheme. It does not establish verified incident rates, causal effects of media portrayal, subgroup differences, media or consumer behavior, political participation, institutional reform effects or a harmonized longitudinal trend; those require the underlying topline, microdata or linked behavioral and episode evidence.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Pew chart page was reviewed for the September 3, 2026 date, 2026 support, discrimination and TV/movie portrayal percentages, historical comparison labels, question notes and survey-source description.
